segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, the dwelling of God is with humankind, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his peoples, and God himself will be with them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more; mourning and crying and pain will be no more. The first things have passed away.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the one seated on the throne said,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Look, I am making all things new.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Write, for these words are faithful and true.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to me,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “They have come to pass. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the one who is thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without cost.

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: The one who conquers will inherit these things, and I will be his God and he will be my son.

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their share will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues came and spoke with me, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain and showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: having the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious stone, like a jasper stone clear as crystal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It had a great, high wall with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates names were inscribed, the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who was speaking with me had a golden measuring rod to measure the city and its gates and its wall.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The city is laid out as a square, its length the same as its width. He measured the city with the rod: twelve thousand stadia. Its length and width and height are equal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also measured its wall: one hundred forty-four cubits by human measure, which is also the angel’s measure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The wall was built of jasper, and the city was pure gold, like pure glass.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every kind of precious stone. The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the fifth sardonyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; each one of the gates was made from a single pearl. And the main street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I saw no sanctuary in it, for its sanctuary is the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The city has no need of the sun or the moon to shine on it, for the glory of God has given it light, and its lamp is the Lamb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Its gates will never be shut by day, for there will be no night there,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they will bring the glory and the honor of the nations into it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

notes.note: In Israel’s Scriptures and in Revelation itself the sea stands for chaos and threat: the beast rises out of it (13:1) and it holds the dead (20:13). Its absence signals the removal of what menaces creation, not a remark about geography. The Greek verb is in the present tense (“is no more”).

The Greek noun is the ordinary word for a tent and recalls the tent-sanctuary in which God accompanied Israel in the wilderness. The verb that follows (“he will dwell”) is from the same root, so “dwelling” and “dwell” are used here to keep the wordplay. Older versions have “tabernacle”; modern versions divide among “tabernacle”, “dwelling” and “home”.

Manuscripts are divided between the plural “peoples” and the singular “people”; the plural, followed here, widens the covenant formula once spoken of Israel to include many peoples. Many manuscripts also add “as their God” at the end of the verse, and most English versions include it. The edition translated here omits it.

The Greek shifts to the present tense (“and he says”) without naming the speaker. The words are assigned here to the one seated on the throne, who speaks before and after. Some interpreters think an angel interjects at this point, as in 19:9 and 22:6, where similar words are spoken.

The Greek verb is plural, unlike the singular “It is done” of 16:17. The subject is most naturally the “words” of verse 5 or the “all things” being made new. Most English versions render it with a singular “It is done”, which obscures the reference.

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle or contest, and “conquer” keeps that note of victory, where “overcome” can now suggest merely getting past a difficulty. Several modern versions also use “conquer” in Revelation. The promise that follows echoes God’s words about David’s heir in 2 Samuel 7:14, here extended to every victor.

The word can mean “unbelieving” (lacking faith) or “unfaithful, untrustworthy”. Placed next to “the cowardly” in a book addressed to churches under pressure to compromise, it probably has in view those who prove disloyal, but “unbelievers” is equally possible and is the more common rendering.

The Greek has no article and could mean “in spirit”, that is, in a visionary state, not bodily. Most translations take it, as here, as a reference to God’s Spirit as the agent of the vision, as in 1:10, 4:2 and 17:3. The scene recalls Ezekiel being set on a very high mountain to see the restored city (Ezekiel 40:2).

A stadion was about 185 meters, so the figure comes to roughly 2,200 kilometers (about 1,400 miles) in each dimension. The number is twelve times a thousand, in keeping with the twelves that run through the chapter, and is generally taken as symbolic. The cube shape recalls the inner room of Solomon’s sanctuary, which was also a perfect cube (1 Kings 6:20).

notes.phrase: one hundred forty-four cubits by human measure, which is also the angel’s measure
notes.note: A cubit was about 45 centimeters, giving roughly 65 meters; the number is twelve times twelve. The text does not say whether this is the wall’s height or its thickness. The closing phrase is terse in Greek (“a human’s measure, which is an angel’s”) and most likely means that the angel used the ordinary human unit.

The modern identity of several of the twelve stones is uncertain, since ancient gem names do not map neatly onto modern mineralogy; the stone called “sapphire”, for example, was probably lapis lazuli. The names are given here in their conventional English forms. The list overlaps substantially with the twelve stones on the high priest’s breastpiece (Exodus 28:17–20).

Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. This translation renders the latter “sanctuary” throughout. Most versions have “temple” here; the point is that the city needs no separate house for God, because God and the Lamb are themselves present.

The Greek word is the same one translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so “nations” is used. The verse draws on Isaiah 60, where nations and kings come to Jerusalem’s light bringing their wealth.

candidates.reason: Traditionally “abomination”; it recurs in the Gospels (“abomination of desolation”), Luke 16:15 and Revelation 17, and the cognate participle in 21:8 should match it.
With πορνεία and πορνεύω it recurs across Paul, Hebrews and Revelation, and versions vary among “fornicator”, “sexually immoral” and “whoremonger”.
The ritual sense (“common, profane, unclean”) recurs in Mark 7, Acts 10–11, Romans 14 and Hebrews, and needs to be distinguished consistently from ἀκάθαρτος.
With φαρμακεία (Galatians 5:20; Revelation 9:21, 18:23, 22:15) it could be rendered “sorcery”, “magic arts” or “drug-potions”, and the family should be handled uniformly.
A divine title occurring nine times in Revelation and in 2 Corinthians 6:18; “Almighty” versus “All-Powerful” or “Ruler of all” should be settled once.
